content.thinking:
I need to carefully plan the whole structure before writing it out in one pass. I'm picturing a koala clinging to a slightly tilted eucalyptus trunk mounted on a base stump, with its chest pressed against the post and limbs wrapped around it for the hug pose.

I'm working out the exact grip positions: trunk offset to the right side at a diagonal lean, koala body centered and facing forward, one arm reaching up to grip high on the trunk, the other crossing the chest to grip lower, and the feet gripping lower still to anchor the pose.

Now I'm pinning down scale and coordinates: koala roughly 0.65m sitting height, trunk about 1.3m on a round wood-slice base, with the koala's bottom resting at about y=0.42 on a thick branch stub jutting from the trunk to support its seated posture.

I'm sketching the body as a chain of bones—hips, lower spine, chest, neck, head—to build a pear-shaped seated bear form, with the hips rooted near the stub and the spine curving up toward the chest and head positions.

Then I add a head joint parented to the neck tip, with a forward-ish direction, and place the head sphere slightly ahead and above that joint to account for the koala's fairly large head size (~0.17 wide, 0.14 tall), centering it around (0.03, 0.98, 0.1).

Now I'm planning the jaw as a small joint parented to the head, offset forward and down slightly, with a black nose pad on the muzzle. For the ears, I'm thinking of using flattened spheres scaled to be round and fluffy, gray with pinkish inner discs, positioned on either side of the head.

Since the "left/right" relative words might not accept negative multipliers safely, I'm deciding to just compute ear positions directly in model space using a literal offset array from the head center coordinates instead of relying on the helper's directional keywords.

Defining ear geometry as flattened spheres with tilt and inward-facing rotation...

Resolving the rotation to a=-s*25°, I work out the inner-ear offset direction so it points outward and forward correctly for both ear sides.

Now I'm planning fur fringe cards on the ears using scattered white fluffy tufts along the rim, filtering hits near the flattened sphere's edge so the tufts only appear where the rim normal is roughly horizontal.

For the body coat I'm setting up a dithered cell-paint gray fur ramp with a countershaded look—darker gray on the back transitioning to cream on the chest—using a noise-based snapped color ramp.

Still writing coat shader logic...

Plotting the body shape as a loft with widening stations from hips up to belly, defining width/height dimensions at each height along the path to get a pear-like torso profile.

Checking the floor alignment: the koala's bum needs to rest on the branch stub, so I'm figuring out how the rounded loft cap at the bottom extends past the starting path point to make sure the bottom sits flush at the right height.

I'll shift the whole koala up by adding a Y offset through a coordinate helper, repositioning everything so the body bottom lands at the correct level relative to the branch stub.

Now I'm reconsidering overall scale though - the total height from bum to head top is coming out too tall for a realistically sized sitting koala (~0.6m), so I need to compress the y-coordinates proportionally rather than just shifting them.

So I'm redesigning with absolute numbers directly: body bottom at 0.43, hips at 0.57, chest at 0.75, neck joint at 0.84, head center at 0.90 with top around 0.97 and ears to ~1.02, giving a total koala height of about 0.6 - and setting body width to roughly 0.26 at its widest to match a realistic koala proportions.

Defining spine chain and body stations...

Working out the head geometry now—building the skull as a scaled sphere with gray cell paint, adding cheek puffs on either side for a wider look, and starting the muzzle shape.

Still placing facial features...

For the eyes, I'm deciding to use small flat-colored boxes instead of spheres to keep the pixel-art aesthetic, giving them a brownish-black texture and sizing them to sit flush against the skull's curved surface near the front of the face.

Keeping eyes small and dark works well. Now I'm working out the ear geometry—positioning, size, and slight rotation for a natural koala look, plus inner pink ear details offset from the ear base for depth.

Adding fringe tufts along the ear rim using scattered pixel-art cards with a soft cream and tan palette, oriented outward along the surface normal to create a textured, fuzzy edge.

Tint logic settled, so now I need to build the body surface before scattering cards on it. Moving to limbs, I'm sketching out the koala's arm placement, working out a trunk path with tilt and curvature to position where the arms attach.

I'm checking clearances: computing trunk surface position at a given height against the koala body's half-width to make sure there's a sensible gap, then thinking about recentering the whole composition — shifting the koala and trunk x-offsets so the combined figure sits centered around x=0 rather than skewed to one side.

I'll apply a constant x-shift to all koala coordinates via a helper function so the body stays consistently offset relative to the trunk, keeping everything wrapped through that shift.

Still working out positions...

I'm shaping the paw with curling fingers that wrap around the trunk's radius, using short curve sweeps from the palm base around the trunk's surface to suggest a gripping hold with claw-tipped digits.

Computing finger positions...

Fingers can sweep along curved paths using a few control points per digit, tapering radius toward the tip. With 4 fingers per hand at 2 joints each plus similar toe counts for feet, the total skeleton lands around 60 joints, which fits the budget comfortably.

I'm adding dark claw tips at finger ends with a near-black color, blending gray paw tones into darker pads via banded gradients along the sweep. The palm gets a flattened sphere scaled slightly for shape, and I'm setting up arm sweeps using a smooth catmull curve through shoulder, elbow, and wrist with tapering radius for a natural limb profile.

Now I'm placing the right arm so it crosses the chest to reach the trunk, working out shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates while checking the elbow clears the body surface and the elbow-to-wrist segment length roughly matches the upper arm length for believable proportions.

Recomputing the wrist position relative to trunk center gives roughly (0.06, 0.72, 0.03), then checking shoulder-to-elbow-to-wrist distances to keep arm segments around 0.19-0.2 each, adjusting elbow placement slightly to avoid overly long segments.

Now working on the left arm: positioning shoulder at the body surface near (0.03, 0.74, 0.0), with elbow reaching forward-up toward the trunk and wrist landing near (0.086, 0.95, 0.005), verifying segment lengths stay close to 0.1 each.

This isn't symmetrical with the right arm by design — the left arm grips close to the trunk while the right crosses over, giving the koala a natural clinging asymmetry, with the head turned to face the viewer. I'm working out finger placement wrapping around the trunk, checking that the wrist offset angle matches the trunk radius, and spreading finger contact points across an angular range from about -50° to 120°.

Now I'm refining the trunk's taper, making its radius shrink gradually from base to top, with the gripping fingers sitting just outside the trunk surface so they read as wrapping around it rather than floating.

Still writing bark texture logic...

Still refining bark and cut-end details...

I should also add dark bark knot chunks and peeling bark flap cards for texture. Thinking about the skeleton structure, I realize the trunk needs proper bone attachment too -- rather than letting trunk meshes default to the hips joint, it'd be cleaner to make a separate "stand" joint as the actual root, positioned at the base, with the koala's hips as a child joint of it.

Setting up the joint hierarchy now: stand as root, hips parented to it, then the spine chain branching off hips with role labels like "spine" for proper rigging.

For the eucalyptus leaves, I'm planning lanceolate curved shapes hanging from thin twigs near the upper trunk, rendered in a pixel-art style with stepped outlines, green cell paint, and a visible midrib vein for detail.

Writing leaf outline geometry...

Working out leaf cell sizing and paint logic now — using the midrib highlight (lighter stripe near the center line) and a green color ramp across the leaf shape to give it some visual depth.

For twig placement, I'm positioning three twigs at different trunk heights, each sweeping outward and down, with leaves hanging off the ends oriented along an outward-downward direction vector and a perpendicular side vector so each leaf's flat plane reads correctly in 3D.

Planning the twig and leaf arrangement: each twig gets 3-4 pendulous leaves distributed along its length, with roll variation applied by rotating the leaf's side vector around its hanging direction, and extra leaves clustered on the lower stub branch. I need to make sure the lowest hanging leaves stay well clear of the floor.

For the stump base, I'm building a short cylinder with painted end-grain rings on top using a radial sine pattern blended with noise, and bark coloring on the sides based on surface normal, sized so its top sits flush and bottom touches the floor.

Now I'm adding scattered moss patches via noise thresholds near the disc edge, plus a few grass tuft cards standing upright at ring positions and some flat fallen leaves lying on the stump surface, building their orientation vectors so the leaf cards lie horizontal rather than vertical.

I'm also placing a handful of small brown eucalyptus gumnuts with caps near the twigs, then working out the koala's hind leg positions -- figuring out where the hips, thighs, and gripping feet should sit relative to the trunk and the stub it's perched on.

I'm placing the ankle near the trunk front-left and checking the hip-knee-ankle distances to make sure the folded leg geometry is consistent, roughly 0.14 and 0.147 units apart.

Now I'm adding a haunch sphere at the hip for thigh mass, and building the left foot with a sole pad, four wrapping toes, and an opposable first toe similar to the hand structure. For the right leg, I'm positioning the hip, knee, and foot so it rests gripping a stub, computing where along that stub (around x=-0.2) the foot should sit by interpolating its y-coordinate.

I'm working out the ankle position so the hip-knee-ankle chain has consistent segment lengths while the foot wraps around the gripping stub, which runs mostly along the x-axis -- so the toes need to wrap in circles in the yz-plane rather than the hand's original wrap pattern, meaning I need a more general wrap function parameterized by center and axis.

Designing wrap function params...

I'm realizing the finger-wrap angles I picked produce digits way too long for a koala paw's scale, so I need to narrow the angular span to get realistic 5-6cm digit lengths instead of the oversized 170° wrap.

For a chunkier style, I settle on finger joints at roughly -35°, 15°, and 65° around the palm sphere, giving about 10cm total span, with each finger built as a two-segment chain parented to the wrist joint. I'm now working out the lateral spacing between fingers based on finger radius and diameter so they don't overlap.

I consider adding an opposable thumb for koala realism but decide to skip it for simplicity, sticking with four straight fingers pointing forward. I'm setting up the color bands for the paw material, assigning gray fur to most of the chain and a darker tone for the claw tips.

Writing chain wrapper function...

For the gray wrist sphere I'll scale it to flatten slightly, then think about claws as darker spike shapes at fingertips and whether a koala needs a visible tail (probably skip it, maybe a small fluffy rump sphere instead). I'm keeping geometry low-poly with sparse segments for that chunky pixel/voxel aesthetic, using cell-painted textures on both boxes and spheres to keep texels square.

Now I'm planning fur cards as small cut-out tufts (roughly 3x4 pixel silhouettes) scattered across the body and cheeks, shaded by face normal to match the pixel texture, plus details like a white chin tuft and pink ear interiors. I'm also filtering where these fur cards can scatter on the head so they avoid the front of the face, and tallying up the total part count across the trunk, bark, twigs, leaves, gumnuts, and koala body pieces.

Fingers for the paws will each use a chain of segments doubled for bands, keeping the mesh count well under budget. For color, I'm defining a grayscale fur ramp and a cream ramp for the chest, then setting up a noisy edge mask so the cream patch blends naturally into the gray fur based on position and surface normal.

Extending the cream mask to cover the lower rump area with a softer transition, while deciding the arms and legs stay gray since the cream rule only applies to torso coordinates—though the crossing arm will naturally pick up some cream near the chest, which actually looks right. Now I'm writing a reusable fur-paint function that takes a cream flag to switch between the two ramps.

For the head, I'm narrowing the cream cutoff to avoid washing out the whole face, keeping it to just the chest region, and planning a separate lighter-gray tone for the cheeks rather than reusing the cream rule there. The head will otherwise use the same gray coat function with matching dither cell size for texture consistency.

Working out texel density now: with roughly 2m² of painted surface on a 1024px sheet, I get about 1.65mm per texel, so a 0.02 fur cell size covers plenty of pixels and the smaller 0.006 leaf cells are still fine too — no need to bump up to 2048. I'll enable dithering on the fur paint call, add a separate shine detail for the nose, skip whiskers since koalas don't have them, and give the eyes a darker squashed patch above them for brow definition.

Now I'm setting up the imports and build function for the koala-on-branch model, pulling in the builder, math/path helpers, and the pixel-paint kit, while being careful to drop unused imports like `pick`. Starting the build function...

Setting up palette and coat paint logic...

Still writing bark paint logic...

Now I'm setting up the stump's top disc with a radial moss pattern based on distance from center and noise thresholds.

Adjusting the trunk path so its base extends slightly below the disc surface, letting it bury into the disc rather than sitting on top.

Still writing trunk geometry...

The trunk sweep parents to the stand bone. Now I'm defining a wrap function for finger joints, working out the axis orientation so that the angle increases toward the correct direction using a cross product between the axis and front vectors.

Writing helper for palm positions...

Still defining finger geometry...

I'm thinking about how the finger base should connect to the palm, and whether to add a palm sphere near the wrist. For consistency I should probably compute the wrist position relative to the trunk wrapper rather than hard-coding coordinates for the hand.

I'm working out the hand and foot joint positions using a shared trunk-wrapper function, deriving the wrist and ankle locations from the hand/palm centers and radius offsets rather than hardcoding each one separately.

Now I'm tracing the arm chain for the left side, computing shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates relative to the body's center and radius so the limb segments connect smoothly into the palm.

Naming the arm joints and figuring out left/right side conventions based on x-coordinate signs, then sketching the sweep radii for the arm tube with tapering thickness from shoulder to wrist.

For the hand I'm adding a palm sphere scaled flatter, then deciding whether fingers should share the same dithered coat material or use a flatter gray with dark claw tips via color bands — leaning toward reusing the coat paint for visual consistency before moving on to the legs.

Now I'm working out hip, knee, and ankle joint positions for the left leg by computing the body's cross-section curve at different heights, checking that the resulting bone lengths stay around 0.15 units, then comparing against where the hands end up relative to the trunk.

For the right leg, I'm setting the hip and knee joints similarly, then figuring out the ankle by tracing a stub path from a trunk point down to a tip, using an axis vector between the two endpoints to position things correctly.

Computing the cross product of the axis with the front vector gives a side vector pointing roughly in +Y, confirming θ=90° corresponds to the top position, which checks out.

Now I'm working through the foot geometry: placing toes at angles curling over the front and top of the foot stub, then positioning the palm point slightly forward to derive the ankle location relative to the center, landing on an approximate ankle coordinate.

Checking the leg proportions, I set the knee position so that hip-to-knee distance is around .14 and knee-to-ankle is around .2 — the shin ends up longer than the thigh, which seems fine for this koala shape. Toe offsets along the foot's stub axis are symmetric at roughly ±0.01 and ±0.03, and I'm mirroring the same wrap angles for the left foot and matching hand.

For the haunches I'm building sphere-based thighs scaled to bulge outward at the front, chaining the hip-knee-ankle joints with a sweep radius that tapers from about .07 down to .04, and capping the feet with slightly flattened spheres. Now I'm moving on to positioning the head's base offset.

Working out neck and spine coordinates... I'm setting the neck as a two-point polyline chain running from the chest tip up to the head, parented to the chest joint, and sweeping it with a radius around .075 so it's thick enough to blend into the head geometry.

Now I'm defining the head joint, parented to the end of the neck chain, pointing up and forward. For the skull itself I'm using a scaled sphere geometry to get a wide koala-like head shape, keeping segment counts low enough for a pixel-art feel, and adding cheek spheres positioned symmetrically on either side of the face.

For the muzzle and nose I'm working out a cream-colored cell-shaded paint with noise-based variation for texture, then sizing and positioning scaled sphere geometries for the muzzle and nose to sit correctly on the face.

Still placing nose details...

Working out the muzzle sphere position and mouth rod geometry, then checking if the lower jaw sphere needs to cover that area.

For the eyes, I'm placing textured boxes on the skull's ellipsoid surface, calculating the local radius at that offset so the eyes sit flush against the curved surface rather than floating or sinking in.

I'll skip the chin tuft and front teeth details, keeping things simple, and add fur fringe cards around the ears and forehead by scattering them across the skull surface. For the body, I'll scatter fur cards over the smooth body sweep surface instead, using small sizes and slight random variation so the triangle count stays low, and pick cream coloring for chest cards from the root paint.

Now I'm shaping a eucalyptus leaf outline using stepped column widths that narrow toward the tip, with slight offsets planned to curve the leaf shape.

Working out the extrusion setup for the leaf shape, I need the direction and side vectors to be orthogonal so the thickness extrudes correctly along the bone — computing the side vector as the cross product with the z-axis to keep it perpendicular to the leaf's direction.

Still defining leaf shading...

Now I'm setting up the twig data structure, defining base points along the trunk and curve paths for each twig, with leaf positions and directions placed at intervals along each one.

Still defining twig placements...

I'm adding small brown gumnut spheres hanging along the twigs, then setting up grass tufts as upward-facing cards arranged in a ring around the disc's edge using a grass texture.

Defining the pixel-art grass pattern with mixed color shades, then placing the tuft cards on top of the disc at scattered angles and radii near its rim, plus a few scattered fallen leaves and bark chunk details on the trunk.

Still defining the paint pattern... then sketching the trunk sweep geometry with tapering radius and flat caps along the two-point path.

Recomputing A at t=0.275 along the trunk gives A=(0.105, 0.40, -0.028), matching the earlier target. I'll add a small leaf cluster at B's tip hanging in a downward-outward direction, and figure out the stub's wrap center by interpolating between A and B where x=-0.19.

For the spine, I'm defining a catmull chain from hips through spine1/spine2 to chest, with hips coincident with the first spine point. Then I'm setting up the body loft across the torso stations using the hips and spine bones, checking that the sweep options support a sides parameter and that the hips joint's position along the path lines up correctly with the station list.

I'm double-checking that the spine chain properly registers spine1 and spine2 as span joints with chest as the tip, confirming the rig's bone assignments for head and body parts, and considering whether to add a small rump sphere for extra fluff near the tail stub. I'm also verifying the root "stand" joint's placement and starting to define the hips joint's parent and role relative to it.

Writing ear geometry code...

Applying the Ry rotation, the z-component works out to roughly +0.46, confirming the ear points forward as expected. Now I'm working out the inner ear position using the same rotated vector offset.

I'm scaling the inner ellipsoid down and checking its offset so it protrudes just slightly past the outer flattened surface rather than bulging out too far—adjusting the offset to around 0.014 to keep it proportionate.

For color, I'll use a pink cell paint ramp blended with noise for subtle variation instead of flat color. Then I'll scatter ear tuft geometry across the ear surface, filtering by normal direction to keep tufts near the rim.

Writing pixel art texture...

I'm making sure the tuft cards tint properly from the coat color since the texture itself is white, and double-checking that all my type imports like `Joint` and `frame` actually exist in their source files before I rely on them.

Setting up imports and helper functions for vectors and palette snapping...

Writing wrapper helper function...

Now working out the wrist and finger placement for the left hand, computing radii along the trunk taper and starting to define a grip helper function for positioning hand geometry...

Still working out joint coordinates...

Checking the right hip position and left leg joint chain—I notice the knee position overlaps the trunk by about 3cm, so I'm adjusting its x-coordinate to pull it clear of the body.

Now I'm computing the right ankle, stub wrapper, and toe placements, verifying the palm sphere radius doesn't collide with the nearest toe point.

Both feet positions check out relative to the body at that height. I'm now placing the thigh blobs, anchoring them to the hip joints with appropriate scale and offset so the legs read correctly from the stub.

Writing the leg sweep geometry and coat coloring, adding a jaw joint with chin positioning, and a thin dark rod for the lip line. Then I'll move on to scattering fluff cards over the chest and body regions, clustering larger cream-colored cards for the chest fluff effect.

Now I'm building the stand disc geometry with a tapered cylinder, defining moss placement rules based on radial distance and noise, and positioning scattered fallen leaf cards flat on the disc surface with proper orientation vectors. I'm also adding small root sweeps flaring from the trunk base down into the disc for a natural anchoring look.

Counting leaf totals from the twigs and stub, confirming the rng usage stays deterministic and single-threaded, and checking that bark scatter happens on the trunk sweep surface before leaves get placed. I'm also double-checking finger and claw coloring, and verifying the sweep call signature with the catmull path source and radius options.

Checking that the bands array of number-fill tuples will type correctly when passed inline since the contextual typing should infer the tuple shapes properly. I'm also confirming the rotation and scale vectors are valid, and setting up the ear surface scatter with rng, min distance, and a filter function for hit placement.

Now I'm defining card parameters for fuzz on ears, grass blades at specific frame positions, and body fur scatter — adjusting size, lean angle, variance, color, and flow direction for each to get the right fur orientation and density.

For cheek fuzz I'm setting the count and minimum distance, filtering out the front-facing area to avoid overlapping with the eyes. Then I'm defining the eye textures (black, brown, white palette) and placing the eye geometry as a small textured box on the head bone, positioned and oriented to face forward with a slight consideration for symmetry between the two eyes.

I'm checking the geometry so the nose sits above and protrudes past the muzzle, which protrudes past the skull front, keeping the koala's facial profile proportional — nose width versus eye spacing checks out, and the overall smooth sphere shapes paired with pixelated textures matches the intended style. Now I'm starting on the gumnut details, defining their shape and brownish color.

Now I'm working out the twig placement around the trunk, adjusting their heights and outward directions so they don't overlap with the trunk's hand/finger bands, nudging a couple of y-positions to avoid clashes.

Still writing twig geometry...

Checking that the twig near the koala head stays clear of the ears, the hanging leaves clear the head top around x≈-0.05, y1.1. Then I'm verifying the left-side sweep twig and starting on the stub leaves with base point near [-0.30, 0.45].

Now I'm double checking type signatures throughout — making sure `frame`, `tip`, `b.joint`, and `b.chain` parent options all line up with their expected Joint/Chain types so nothing breaks at compile time.

The sweep and detail work for the body, head, and ears looks consistent, so I shift to verifying the fur and skin-shading expressions — checking that `noise`, `c.pick`, and the cream color rule use the correct coordinate references around the center x value.

Now I'm writing a helper function for generating finger joints that builds a chain of digit segments using wrapped offsets and angles, then sweeps a tapered profile with a claw band at the tip along each finger.

I'm double-checking naming consistency across chains and joints, confirming unique prefixes for hands and feet, and verifying the digit role assignment and parent linkage to hips for the leg chains. I'm also making a final pass to ensure variables like TAX, T1, rand, and FUR are all actually used before finalizing the write.

Now I'm defining the cut disc geometry as a short cylinder positioned along the TAX direction offset from T1, and setting up cutPaint to measure distance from T1 for its coloring logic, before assembling the final output.
